source.title: Automated Neuron Labelling Enables Generative Steering and Interpretability in Protein Language Models
source.authors: Arjun Banerjee; David Martinez; Camille Dang; Ethan Tam

record.file_problem: None noted; the text includes apparent naming and model-size inconsistencies, but is otherwise a complete paper.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes how neuron labels and attributed protein features vary across protein-language-model sizes, but it does not test held-out cross-entropy scaling, loss extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or any other listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The paper's own scaling-related results concern neuron-label and feature distributions, not pretraining loss or power-law fits. It also reports protein-generation and steering outcomes, which do not test the listed scaling claims. References to scaling laws from other work are not study results.
record.test_reason: The paper labels neurons in ESM-2 protein language models and describes, qualitatively from figures, how labelled feature coverage and layer distribution differ across model sizes. It calls this a 'PLM scaling law', but it reports no loss, no power-law fit, no compute or token sweep, and no downstream-task performance against scale. None of V1–V7 is tested. The size-dependent neuron-label findings are a different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors say neuron-label analysis across model sizes suggests 'elementary scaling laws': bigger PLMs capture more fine-grained features, and features spread more across layers. They note that only three models were labelled. The record could add that this 'scaling law' is qualitative and figure-based, with no fitted law.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies neuron labeling and protein generation in protein language models rather than the loss-scaling methods in the original sources.

fits_no_version.finding: The text says the 3B model's neuron labels cover hands, supercoiling and fingers, while the 8M model's cover only fingers (Figure 8, qualitative).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger protein language models have neurons attributable to more fine-grained structural features.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger models show more distributed layer placement of functional-feature labels; ESM-8M concentrates functional features in the final sextile (Figure 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The depth distribution of interpretable features in PLMs changes with model size.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors state that increasing parameter size gives a greater frequency of feature-attributed neurons. No numbers are given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The fraction of neurons with attributable biological features rises with PLM size.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the Workshop on Generative AI for Biology at ICML 2025, PMLR 267
record.problems: The scaling-related findings are qualitative descriptions of figures, with no numeric fit or uncertainty reported in the text. The model-size and model-name descriptions are inconsistent in places, and the authors state that only three models were labeled.
record.rows_left_out: Protein-generation and steering results were omitted because they do not measure any listed scaling-claim outcome.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss measured across parameters, tokens or compute.
Protein models are studied, but no power-law fit of loss or any metric is made.
No downstream task performance is measured against scale or loss. The steering results are not compared across sizes as a scaling trend.
No exponents or fits are reported.

record.verdict_notes: The paper uses 'scaling law' loosely, to mean a qualitative size trend in neuron labels, not a loss power law. The model names in Section 4 are garbled (three '8B' listings). The reader's T6/discusses classification and its omission of the steering rows are appropriate.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No test of loss predictions from small runs against larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation experiment or fitted growth trends for parameters and tokens.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The paper studies protein language models, but does not test whether the claimed power-law form holds for their loss or across training regimes.
No downstream-task performance relationship with model scale or pretraining loss is tested.
No analysis of loss-law exponents, fitting choices, compute-optimal splits, or departures from a power law.

rows.subject: ESM-8M
rows.stage_stated: pretrained protein language model; training stage not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared neuron-label feature coverage across differently sized ESM variants.
rows.measure: Whether labels captured structural details including hands, supercoiling, and fingers
rows.value: The paper says ESM-8M captures fingers, while the 3B model captures hands, supercoiling, and fingers; figure values are not stated in text.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes this qualitative comparison, but it is about neuron-label feature coverage, not loss scaling.
rows.check: Measures neuron-label feature coverage, not loss or downstream performance. Model naming in Section 4 is inconsistent (lists 'esm2 t36 8B', 'esm2 t12 8B'), while the text refers to 8M, 35M and 3B. The subject size should be treated as uncertain.

rows.subject: ESM-3B
rows.stage_stated: pretrained protein language model; training stage not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared neuron-label feature coverage across differently sized ESM variants.
rows.measure: Whether labels captured structural details including hands, supercoiling, and fingers
rows.value: The paper says ESM-3B captures hands, supercoiling, and fingers; the 8M model captures fingers. Figure values are not stated in text.
rows.note: This is a qualitative result about labeled neuron features, not held-out loss.
rows.check: Same as r1. The 3B identity is inferred from the prose, but Section 4 lists the models inconsistently.

rows.subject: ESM-8M
rows.stage_stated: pretrained protein language model; training stage not stated
rows.operation_detail: Examined the relative distribution of neuron labels across layer sextiles.
rows.measure: Relative occurrence of feature-attributed neurons by layer
rows.value: The text says sequence-derived features peak in the first sextile and fall off afterward, while functional features are concentrated in the final sextile; figure values are not stated in text.
rows.note: The result concerns where neuron labels occur within a model, not loss as a function of scale.
rows.check: Layer-sextile distribution of labels within one model. This is not a scaling measure of any version.

rows.subject: ESM-3B
rows.stage_stated: pretrained protein language model; training stage not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared relative distributions of feature-attributed neurons across ESM variants and layer sextiles.
rows.measure: Relative occurrence of functional-feature labels across layer sextiles
rows.baseline: ESM-8M and ESM-35M are the stated comparison models; numeric baselines not stated.
rows.value: The text says functional features appear in earlier sextiles in ESM-3B than in the two smaller models; figure values are not stated in text.
rows.note: The paper describes this as a change in feature distribution with model size, not as a loss-scaling result.
rows.check: Size-dependent label distribution across depth, not loss or task performance. The numbers_found value '1/1' is unexplained, and no number appears in the text.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
